searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's; one left unspent. One shared search, restricted to the consorzio's and the ministry's domains, settled the DOC of 1966, the DOCG of 1980 and the ageing rules of both DOCGs for every record. Four were restricted to a primary body's or a house's own domain (langhevini.it with the ministry once, produttoridelbarbaresco.com three times) and are read as primary through their summaries; the house sheets of Gaja reached through its importer's file host are counted as the house's own sheets. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; nothing that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification and its year, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).
The searches went first to the dates, the people, the sites and the making; a fact the Codex library states stood on the library unless a search contradicted it.

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a claim rested on one account only it was softened or cut, and one cut (Costa Russi's 1978) was restored when a second search found the house's own sheet.
Sources whose address or title carries a writer's name (a wine wiki under a first name, a critic's byline) were read in the results but never cited.

tested: Founding and the generations: 1859 by Giovanni Gaja in most accounts (the importer, Wikipedia, Glengarry); the importer counts five generations in all, the founder among them, and the great grandson, born 1940, joined in 1961 at twenty one: the founding and the 1961 confirmed, the count changed.

The village wine: fourteen vineyards in the house's 2023 sheet, Lamuse and the trade; the house has bought no grapes since 1961 by iDealwine, Tastingbook and Lamuse: confirmed, and with it the question's key against bought grapes.

The making: fermented in steel, each lot twelve months in oak, blended, then twelve months more (the house's sheet and the Kwast report); Vinove alone gives six months in barrique and eighteen in large casks: the twelve and twelve kept, the share of new barriques cut.

The crus: Sori San Lorenzo first made in 1967 (Vinous, Jeroboams), Sori Tildin in 1970 (the house's 2023 sheet through the importer), Costa Russi in 1978 (the house's 2023 Costa Russi sheet and the importer's pages): confirmed after one cut and its restoration.
Darmagi: Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1978, the name from the father's exclamation, told by the house's sheets and the importer as a family story: confirmed and hedged.

The Langhe years: the three crus outside the DOCG from 1996 with about five per cent Barbera, back to Barbaresco as Nebbiolo alone from 2013, the daughter's decision with her father's assent (Decanter, Lay and Wheeler): confirmed, and under the next generation stands.
The rules: Barbaresco DOCG in 1980, at least twenty six months, nine in wood, from 1 November of the harvest year (the consorzio and the regulation): confirmed.
The house rules: nobody living named (the great grandson, his father and the daughter are described); no price or score; British spelling; no dash.

tested: The founding: a tavern opened in 1908 at San Giuseppe near Monforte d'Alba (Liv-ex and a second account), the Wine Scholar Guild calling the year unclear: the hedge stands.
The first Monfortino: the founder's son back from the First World War and his first estate Riserva of 1920 (the Wine Scholar Guild), 1924 elsewhere: the 1920s by most accounts stands.
Cascina Francia: bought by the elder brother in 1974, every wine from it from 1978, the label shortened to Francia from the 2010 vintage (Rare Wine Co, the Wine Scholar Guild, Wikipedia): confirmed.

Arione: the 2015 Monfortino the first with Arione fruit, about a fifth of it (Museum Wines, Gute Weine, Grand Cru Wijnen and the Wine Advocate note they carry): changed from joining from 2015 on to first added in 2015.

The making: open topped wooden vats and four to five weeks on the skins (Decanter's Wine Legend, up to five weeks; the importer's sheet, about four); no temperature control in the Wine Legend, but Decanter's producer profile has the father welcoming it to prolong a cool maceration: the claim cut.

The cask: Monfortino at least seven years in large casks and Francia about four (the importer's sheet, Decanter, a 2020 Francia listing); the 2015 Monfortino about five years by merchants: some seven years stands.
The 1969 division and the riserva rules (sixty two months, eighteen in wood, from 1 November of the harvest year, by the regulation): confirmed.
The house rules: the founder, his son, the two brothers and the grandson described, nobody living named; no price, score or production; British; no dash.

tested: The founding: 1919 by Giulio Mascarello in most accounts, 1918 with his father Bartolomeo in one, 1 January 1920 by A Wine Atlas of the Langhe in another (Wikipedia, the Wine Scholar Guild, merchants): the library's 1919 kept, the story widened.

Bartolo: joined the family firm, Cantina Mascarello, in 1945 and learned from his father, who had learned from his own (Wikipedia and a merchant's profile); died on 12 March 2005 at seventy eight by the obituaries; born 1926 or 1927: confirmed, dated by his death.

The label: hand painted, No Barrique, No Berlusconi, in the 2001 election campaign, carabinieri at an Alba shop, Decanter's report of 2002 (Decanter, Wikipedia, a merchant's story): changed from the prime minister of the day and the early 2000s.

The making: cement tanks, native yeasts, no temperature control, a long submerged cap maceration of thirty to fifty days, some thirty months to three years in Slavonian botti (the importer's sheets, a merchant's 2021 note, Vinous): confirmed.
The sites: Cannubi, San Lorenzo and Rue in Barolo with Rocche dell'Annunziata in La Morra (the importer's 2021 sheet and the library): confirmed.
The others: Dolcetto d'Alba and Langhe Freisa among the house's wines (the importer's sheet): confirmed, Freisa named as the label names it.
The house rules: Bartolo's father and daughter described; Berlusconi now named with his dates, dead in 2023; no price or score; British; no dash.

changed.why: The accounts give 1918, 1919 and 1920, and credit the grandfather's teaching; the building of the cellar rests on one account.

tested: Falletto: bought in 1982 in most accounts (Superiore, Rare Wine Co), 1980 in Mtouton: the early 1980s stands. Le Rocche the upper part, south to south west, calcareous clay (Superiore, Mtouton): confirmed. Azienda Agricola Falletto for the house's own vines and Casa Vinicola Bruno Giacosa for bought grapes, the red label for the Riserva and the white for the rest (Rare Wine Co, Superiore): confirmed.

Bruno: born 1929, working with his father Mario, his grandfather Carlo having made wine in Neive (Decanter's Wine Legend, Wikipedia); died on 21 January 2018 (Wikipedia, and Dissapore by the author): confirmed; the age of thirteen found nowhere, cut.
Santo Stefano: his first declared single vineyard wine, the 1964 Barbaresco Riserva Speciale (Vinous; Castello di Neive's own page dates Cru Santo Stefano on both labels to 1964): confirmed.
Asili and Rabaja: bought in 1996 (Decanter, Gambero Rosso), the 1990s or early 1990s elsewhere: changed from the late 1990s to 1996.

The cask: thirty to thirty six months in large French oak casks (Bindella, the house's listings of 2012 and 2014, Vino.com); the bottle time twenty seven or thirty six months in the house's listings, more than two years by Superiore, eight months by Bindella: the cask widened, the bottle time cut to a rest in bottle.
The founding: 1890, a cellar bought in Neive in 1895 by the house's account as a merchant relays it, and 1900 (Wein.plus, Gourmet Hunters, the library): left empty, as the author left it.
The 2006 vintage: no Barolo or Barbaresco bottled, the wine sold in bulk (Decanter's news of 2009 and its feature on the vintage, a second trade report): added to the story.
The house rules: Bruno named with his dates, his daughter described; no price or score; British; no dash.

tested: The cellar of 1894: Domizio Cavazza, head of Alba's school of oenology and owner of the castle, gathering nine landowners in the castle cellars (the house's story); shut in the 1920s by the house and the 1930s by a trade account: hedged.

The cooperative of 1958: the parish priest, come to the village after the Second World War, bringing together nineteen farmers or families; the first vintage made in the courtyard of his house with second hand equipment, most sold in bulk the next spring to pay for the cellar at the foot of the tower, finished in 1960 (the house's story and its page on the priest): confirmed; the priest's worry about families leaving the land found nowhere, cut.

The crus: Asili, Pora, Ovello and Moccagatta among the first single vineyards of 1967 (the house's cru pages), Rio Sordo from 1978, Paje regular from 1982; nine crus made only in vintages judged excellent, Riserva after four years (the production style page); the Rabaja Riserva thirty months in large casks (its 2021 sheet): confirmed.

The making: steel, twenty four days at 28 degrees Celsius, pumping over two or three times a day (the house's Barbaresco page): changed from some four weeks to three to four weeks; the page gives no cask length or size.
The rules: DOC in 1966, DOCG in 1980, twenty six months with nine in wood (the consorzio and the regulation): confirmed.
The house rules: the founder of 1894 and the priest described, nobody living named; members, hectares and bottles left out; the table line's ranking softened; British; no dash.
